summary:
**A.P.E.X.—Space Explorers** is an interactive educational website designed mainly for children aged 7–15 but accessible to all age groups.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge **"Abandoned but Not Forgotten",** the project brings the stories of spacecraft and rovers left behind on the Moon and Mars to life.

NASA already provides detailed information about these missions through its NSSDCA archives, but much of it can be difficult for young children to understand.

To address this problem, I built a website where spacecraft **tell their own stories** through animations, narration, subtitles, and simple explanations.

The website includes 5 animated stories, 15 interactive mission cards, 70 fun facts, and interactive models of the Saturn V rocket and James Webb Space Telescope.

My goal is to make NASA's scientific information easier for children to explore and understand while helping them discover the important contributions these spacecraft made to science.

Team, who developed the educational concept and reviewed all final outputs. During production, OpenAI ChatGPT was used to assist with frontend development (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and interface design, while Google Gemini was used to generate the introductory video for the spacecraft storytelling experience.
details:
A.P.E.X. — Space Explorers

About My Project

A.P.E.X. — Space Explorers is an interactive educational website I built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten."

The challenge focuses on spacecraft and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Although these machines may have stopped working, they made important discoveries and helped scientists understand space better.

The main objective was to tell their stories in a way that children could easily understand.

Why I Built It

NASA already provides a large amount of information about these missions through its NSSDCA archives and other websites.

However, much of this information contains difficult scientific words and detailed explanations that younger children may struggle to understand.

The problem is not that information is unavailable. The problem is that it is not always easy to understand.

That is why I created A.P.E.X., mainly for children aged 7–15, while keeping it accessible to other age groups.

What I Have Built

Instead of creating a normal website with long articles, I built a website where spacecraft tell their own stories.

Children can choose the Moon, Mars, or other places and explore different missions.

The website currently includes:

  • 5 animated stories: Eagle, Intrepid, Falcon, Sojourner, and the Viking Twins.
  • 15 interactive mission fact files covering spacecraft from the Moon, Mars, and other destinations.
  • 70 fun facts about 14 spacecraft, with an option to hear the facts aloud.
  • An interactive Saturn V rocket, where children can explore its parts and listen to simple explanations.
  • An interactive James Webb Space Telescope, where children can select different parts to learn how they work.

The stories include animations, narration, pictures, and subtitles.

Each story helps children understand what the spacecraft was, why it was sent into space, what it discovered, and what happened after its mission ended.

How My Website Is Different

The main difference is how the information is presented.

Instead of just reading about a spacecraft, children can listen to the spacecraft explain its own journey.

For example, Sojourner tells its story as a rover exploring Mars, while the Moon stories introduce children to the spacecraft that helped astronauts explore the lunar surface.

I also wanted children to have a choice. They can watch a complete story, explore a shorter mission card, or discover something through fun facts.

The website is designed so that children can learn at their own pace.

Tools and Resources I Used

I developed the website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI assistance from ChatGPT and Codex for coding, design, and improvements.

I also used AI-assisted illustrations, animations, and narration, including HeyGen-generated voices.

NASA's NSSDCA records, NASA and JPL mission histories, and photographs were used to support the stories.

The website includes a Sources and Credits section explaining the references, media, and AI tools used.

What Impact Do I Want to Create?

My main goal is to make real space mission information easier for children to understand.

Without A.P.E.X., a child may need to read several technical pages to learn about a spacecraft.

With A.P.E.X., they can choose a spacecraft, hear its story, explore its journey, and learn about its discoveries in one place.

I want children to become more curious about science and understand how these spacecraft contributed to space exploration.

The website is a working educational project. In the future, I would like to test it with children, measure what they learn, and add more stories and activities.

My goal is not to replace NASA's information, but to make that information simpler, more interesting, and easier for the next generation to understand.

The spacecraft may have completed their missions, but their contributions to science should never be forgotten.
